title: The last hour
hookLine: bright screens late tend to push sleep later

cards: Before electric light, evenings ended with the sun. It went down. There was firelight, maybe a lamp, then the dark.
Then, in a blink, came electric light, then television, then a bright little screen held six inches from your face in bed.
Your body's clock is much older than any of that, and it still reads light as a message: it's daytime, stay up. Yesterday was the bedtime. Today is the hour before it, the runway sleep lands on.

teach.b: As evening comes and light fades, your brain starts releasing melatonin, a hormone that tells the body night has arrived.

Bright light, especially the bluish light screens and many bulbs give off, can hold that signal back. In the early two thousands, scientists found special cells in the eye whose main job isn't seeing shapes at all.
They measure light and report to the body's clock. Then came a study at Harvard, published in 2015.
For five nights, people read on a light-emitting e-reader before bed; for five other nights, a printed book.
After the screen, they took longer to fall asleep, their melatonin came later, and they felt less alert the next morning. It was a lab study with a small group, so it's a clue, not a verdict.
And light isn't the only thing: a gripping show or a tense group chat wakes the mind up too, whatever the color of the screen. Night mode may help a little; it doesn't make the scroll restful.
So the practice here is gentle and old. Let the last hour look a bit more like the old evenings. Lamps instead of overhead lights.
Screens off, or at least far away.
Something slow in your hands: a book, a cup, a conversation, a stretch. You're not fighting the day. You're dimming it, the way the sky does, a little at a time.

how: Sleep specialists often suggest a wind-down hour before bed with lower light, fewer screens and a calm routine, sometimes called sleep hygiene.

games.q: it's one hour before your bedtime. the overhead lights are on and your phone is in your hand. what does the practice suggest?
o: switch to night mode and keep going.
lamps on, phone out of reach.
turn every light off and lie there.
games.why: lamps instead of overhead lights, the screen out of reach, something slow in your hands. dim the day, a little at a time.

practice: Take your bedtime and count back one hour, then picture that moment: which lights go off, and which lamp stays on?
Where does the phone go, charging in another room or face down across this one, and what slow thing will you hold instead? See it clearly, as if it's already evening.

wordCard.voice: Melatonin, the hormone released as light fades that tells the body night has arrived. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: dim the day. Sleep needs a runway to land on. That's day one hundred thirty-six.
